findings.summary: The case fundamentals that make page 1's rules meaningful — glob patterns, first-match-wins, and `|` alternation — are taught a full page after the consequences that depend on them.
findings.evidence: Page 1 asserts "`*)` is the catch-all default. Placed in the middle it swallows everything, and every branch after it is dead code" and shows `-h|--help) usage ;;` / `-*) die "unknown $1" ;;`; only on page 2 does the learner meet "Tested top to bottom; the **first** hit runs, then stop", "Alternation `start|begin|up)` matches any of the three", and "Glob syntax only" / "`*` any string, even empty".
findings.fix: Swap the case sections: put page 2's "Patterns Are Globs, Not Regex" and "First Match Wins" blocks before page 1's "Ordering Kills" / "Branch Terminators" blocks, so top-to-bottom matching and `*` semantics are established before the `*)`-last rule, `;&`/`;;&`, and the `-h|--help` example.

findings.summary: A six-part numbered sequence on lexicographic `<`/`>` opens on page 6 under an unrelated page title, so the learner meets "1. What They Compare" with no antecedent for "They".
findings.evidence: Page 6 is titled "set -e, Exit Codes & Verification" and, immediately after the "One-Line Recall" sidebox, runs "1. What They Compare" and "2. No Escaping in [[ ]]"; the matching title and subtitle — "Lexicographic < and >" / "Sorting Text, Not Math" — appear only on page 7, which starts at "3. But [ ] Needs \<".
findings.fix: Move sections 1 and 2 onto page 7 so all six numbered sections sit under the "Lexicographic < and >" title, and let page 6 end at "Verify Before You Ship" / "One-Line Recall".

findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a bare series label with no hook, burying the actual hook in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of BASH CONTROL FLOW. `[[ 10 > 9 ]]` is false, and that one line has broken more deploy scripts than any missing semicolon." — Part 1's caption opens directly with the `[[ 10 > 9 ]]` line; Part 2 prefixes it with a label that carries no hook.
findings.fix: Open with the hook and move the part label to the end: "`[[ 10 > 9 ]]` is false, and that one line has broken more deploy scripts than any missing semicolon. … (Part 2 of BASH CONTROL FLOW.)"
Run the fit pass — it adds material from the book without removing anything.

findings.summary: Page 3 opens with orphaned bullets that continue page 1's field-splitting example, with an entire case chapter separating them.
findings.evidence: Page 3's first block begins "Extra fields all land in the LAST variable" with no preceding heading or code; the `read` call it describes is page 1's final block, `while IFS=: read -r user pass uid rest; do` ... `done < /etc/passwd   # rest = all leftovers`.
findings.fix: Move the "Extra fields" / `exec 3<` / `read -u 3` bullets to page 1 immediately beneath the `/etc/passwd` example (or move that example to the head of page 3), and give page 3 a real opening heading.

findings.summary: The code block under "Why does my counter print 0?" is clipped at the block's right edge, cutting a command mid-word.
findings.evidence: Line renders as `while read l; do ((c++)); done < <(gre` — the substitution `<(grep ...)` is severed at the code-block border, and the following line `echo $c  # correct now` wraps beneath it.
findings.fix: Shorten the snippet (e.g. `done < <(grep x f)` on its own line) or enable wrapping/reduce font size so the full line fits inside the block width.

findings.summary: Page 4 closes with three bullets whose subjects (`b`, `c`, brace expansion) are never introduced until page 5's table.
findings.evidence: Page 4's final bullets read "If `b` fails, `c` runs too — a classic silent bug" and "Braces expand before variables; use C-style `for`"; the constructs they explain first appear on page 5 as table rows ["`a && b || c`","not if/else"] and ["`{1..$n}`","never expands"].
findings.fix: Delete the trailing bullet block from page 4 and attach those three explanations directly under page 5's "Two More Silent Ones" table, where `a && b || c`, `{1..$n}`, and the tight poll loop are named.

findings.summary: Nodes and connector lines in the "Pick the Loop" flowchart overlap each other, with text running over box borders.
findings.evidence: The label `glob: for f in *` crosses its own node border (the leading `glob:` sits on the rule), and a vertical connector is drawn straight through the text of `for (( i=0; i<n; i++ ))` between `i=0;` and `i<n`.
findings.fix: Increase the flowchart's node spacing / lane widths so edges route between nodes instead of through them, and pad node boxes so labels sit fully inside their borders.

findings.summary: Page 6 shows the `[ a < b ]` redirection trap as a bare example under a `[[ ]]` heading, one page before page 7 explains why it happens.
findings.evidence: Under "2. No Escaping in [[ ]]", page 6 prints "[ a < b ]      # opens file b!" with only the note "unescaped < is a redirection"; the reason — "`[` is a ==command==, so `<` is parsed as a **redirect**" and "`[ a < b ]` redirects stdin from the file `b`" — arrives on page 7 under "3. But [ ] Needs \<".
findings.fix: Move that three-line `[ ]` code block from page 6 to page 7 as the example for section 3, leaving section 2 to show only `[[ ]]` behaviour.

findings.summary: New teaching material is introduced after the handbook's closing summary pages, so the part reads as if it ended and then restarted.
findings.evidence: Page 5 delivers the wrap-up — "Pick the Test", "Pick the Loop", "Defensive Header", the "Truthiness Recap" takeaway and "Quoting Rule of Thumb" — and page 6 ends with the "One-Line Recall" sidebox, yet pages 6–7 then open a fresh six-section lesson on lexicographic comparison.
findings.fix: Relocate the whole "Lexicographic < and >" lesson to before page 5 (it belongs with the `[[ ]]` vs `[ ]` vs `(( ))` comparison material), leaving pages 5 and 6's summary/verification blocks as the final pages.

findings.summary: The title "set -e, Exit Codes & Verification" describes only the first half of the page; the second half is the lexicographic `<`/`>` sequence, which the title never mentions.
findings.evidence: Page 6 blocks after the "One-Line Recall" sidebox: heading "1. What They Compare" ("Inside `[[ ]]`, `<` and `>` compare ==strings==, never numbers"), heading "2. No Escaping in [[ ]]", plus three code blocks — 6 of the page's 13 blocks — while page 7 is titled "Lexicographic < and >" and opens at "3. But [ ] Needs \<".
findings.fix: Retitle page 6 to cover both halves, e.g. "set -e, Exit Codes & Lexicographic < >", or move the "1."/"2." lexicographic blocks onto page 7 so each title matches its page.

findings.summary: The "Escaping Is the Tell" callout misstates what a backslash does inside `[[ ]]` — bash does not perform a comparison against a literal `\<`, it rejects the expression.
findings.evidence: "In `[[ ]]` the backslash is wrong — it makes Bash compare against the literal `\<`." In `[[ a \< b ]]` the quoted `\<` is no longer recognised as a binary operator, so bash aborts parsing the conditional (`syntax error in conditional expression` / `conditional binary operator expected`) — there is no operator left to compare anything with. ShellCheck SC2075 states it the same way: "`[[` is considered its own grammatical construct, and therefore it does not require (nor does it allow) escaping `<` or `>`."
findings.fix: Reword to: "In `[[ ]]` the backslash is wrong — `[[ a \< b ]]` is a syntax error (`conditional binary operator expected`), because quoting the operator stops Bash recognising it. Write `<` bare."

findings.summary: The caption claims ten pages, but this part contains seven — the text was carried over unchanged from Part 1, which does have ten.
findings.evidence: caption: "Ten pages of dense field notes, plus the gotchas that corrupt scripts without ever printing an error." This part's `slides` array holds 7 pages ("case Dispatch & the read -r Loop" … "Lexicographic < and >"); `parts/01/post.json` has 10 page_title entries and the identical caption sentence.
findings.fix: Change to "Seven pages of dense field notes" for Part 2 (or phrase it as "Part 2 of a seventeen-page handbook").

findings.summary: The "Ans→" marker on the Q&A callouts renders at a few pixels tall and is illegible.
findings.evidence: Under "Why does my counter print 0?" (page 4) and "Why did my test create an empty file?" (page 7), the lead-in reads as an unreadable smudge approximately 5 px high versus ~22 px body text.
findings.fix: Set the answer-marker text at a minimum of body-text size (or drop it and rely on the bullet list) so it is readable at render resolution.

findings.summary: The `find -print0` rename recipe substitutes spaces in the whole path, including directory components, so it fails on any directory whose name contains a space.
findings.evidence: "find . -print0 | while IFS= read -rd '' f; do / mv -- \"$f\" \"${f// /_}\" / done  # survives newlines in filenames" — for `./my dir/a b.txt` the target expands to `./my_dir/a_b.txt`, a directory that does not exist, and `mv` errors with "No such file or directory".
findings.fix: Rename only the basename, e.g. `d=${f%/*}; b=${f##*/}; mv -- "$f" "$d/${b// /_}"` (and add `-depth` to `find` so directories are renamed after their contents).

findings.summary: Page 1 presents a `find | while read` pipeline as a model idiom two pages before the reader learns that piping into `while` creates a subshell.
findings.evidence: Page 1: "find . -print0 | while IFS= read -rd '' f; do" ... "# survives newlines in filenames"; page 3 then warns "cmd | while" → "loop runs in a subshell" / "variable writes vanish", and page 4 calls the same shape "the pipe made a subshell".
findings.fix: Either add a one-line note to the `find` example that the pipe is safe only because the body sets no variables, or rewrite it as `while IFS= read -rd '' f; do ... done < <(find . -print0)` to match the idiom taught later.

findings.summary: Two exit-status bullets are stranded at the end of the summary page, ahead of the exit-status page they belong to.
findings.evidence: Page 5's last block is "`128+N` encodes death by signal `N`" / "Capture it at once: `rc=$?` — next command overwrites it", with no heading; page 6 then presents the table rows ["`130`","Ctrl-C, 128+2"] and ["`137`","SIGKILL, 128+9"].
findings.fix: Move both bullets to page 6 directly above the "Status Codes to Recognise" table, under that heading.

findings.summary: The example comment `[[ B < a ]] # ASCII order` asserts byte ordering for `[[ ]]`, which the deck itself contradicts two pages later and which is false in any non-C locale.
findings.evidence: Page 6: "`[[ B < a ]]       # ASCII order`" versus page 7: "`[[ ]]` sorts by the current ==LC_COLLATE==, not raw bytes" and "`LC_COLLATE=en_US.UTF-8` / `[[ B < a ]]    # false, aAbB`". Since bash 4.1, `<`/`>` in `[[ ]]` use `strcoll()` (the manual: "When used with `[[`, the '<' and '>' operators sort lexicographically using the current locale"), so the same line is true under `LC_ALL=C` and false under `en_US.UTF-8`.
findings.fix: Change the comment to name the locale, e.g. `[[ B < a ]]      # true under LC_ALL=C only`, or replace the line with a locale-independent pair such as `[[ abc < abd ]]`.
